nameStory: The 'Ice Thorn' name likely comes from this tiny snail's crystalline, translucent shell that can look like a miniature icicle when caught in the right light. Its scientific name 'exile' suggests something banished or remote, fitting for a species so small and elusive that it's easy to overlook in the leaf litter where it lives.
description: Ice Thorn is one of New England's tiniest land snails, so small you could fit several on your pinky nail. This microscopic mollusk has a delicate, cone-shaped shell that's nearly transparent and reaches only about 2 millimeters tall. It's a member of the hollow-shelled snail family, creatures that bridge the gap between land and water in their evolutionary history. Despite its diminutive size, it's a complete snail with all the usual parts, just shrunk down to almost invisible proportions.

idTips.label: Shell size
idTips.description: Incredibly tiny at only 1.5-2mm tall - smaller than most grains of rice and easily mistaken for a bit of debris

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Elongated cone or bullet-shaped, much taller than it is wide, tapering to a sharp point at the top

idTips.label: Shell color
idTips.description: Nearly colorless to pale amber, so translucent you can sometimes see the animal's body through the shell wall

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Smooth and glossy when fresh, feeling almost glassy if you can manage to touch something so small

idTips.label: Whorl count
idTips.description: Usually 4-5 whorls (spiral turns) that are relatively flat against each other, not deeply separated

idTips.label: Aperture shape
idTips.description: Opening is oval with a slightly thickened lip, taking up about 1/3 of the total shell height

habitat: Look for Ice Thorn in consistently moist leaf litter, particularly in deciduous and mixed forests where fallen leaves stay damp year-round. They prefer areas with rich organic soil near streams, springs, or other water sources, often hiding under logs, stones, or deep in decomposing vegetation. **[UNCERTAIN]** - Limited observation data makes habitat preferences speculative.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm and moisture increases from snowmelt. Look in freshly dampened leaf litter as they emerge to feed on decomposing organic matter.
seasonality.summer: May retreat deeper into soil and under logs during dry spells. Best found after rain when they come closer to the surface to graze on fungi and bacteria.
seasonality.fall: Active again as leaves fall and create fresh habitat. This may be the best time to spot them as they feed on newly decomposing material.
seasonality.winter: Likely inactive, sheltering deep in soil or under insulating leaf litter. **[UNCERTAIN]** - Winter behavior poorly documented for this species.

funFact: With only one confirmed observation recorded in all of New England, finding an Ice Thorn snail would make you part of an extremely exclusive club - you'd be among the first people to document this species in our region in recent memory!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other minute snails in leaf litter, or simply overlooked entirely as a speck of debris. The Herald-snail (Carychium minimum) is similar but typically shorter and more robust-looking, while Ice Thorn is more elongated and needle-like.
contextualKnowledge: The extremely low observation count (just 1 in New England) suggests this species is either incredibly rare in our region, very recently discovered here, or so small and cryptic that it's been overlooked by most naturalists. **[UNCERTAIN]** - Species status and distribution data should be verified.
compareHints: Ice Thorn differs from its relative the Herald-snail by being more elongated and narrow, like comparing a bullet to a teardrop. **[UNCERTAIN]** - Direct comparison details are speculative due to limited data. Both are incredibly small, but Ice Thorn's more stretched-out proportions and slightly larger size help distinguish it when viewed under magnification.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Herald-snail differs from its close relative the Ice Thorn (Carychium exile) primarily in size and shell proportions, though both are so tiny that distinguishing them usually requires microscopic examination.
